articles.content: A century after her mysterious 11-day disappearance, the Queen of Crime is everywhere. With an exhibition at the British Library, a new Miss Marple novel and a hot young Poirot hitting the screen, how did the novelist become such big business? On the evening of 4 December 1926, Teresa Neele checked into the Swan Hydropathic hotel in Harrogate. A tall, attractive woman in her mid-30s with reddish hair and grey eyes, she had travelled from South Africa and carried just cash, a comb, a hot-water bottle and a photograph of a boy, the name Teddy written on the back. At dinner she told a guest that her daughter had died, and later danced the Charleston – “not very well”, according to those who were there. Neele spent the next 10 days shopping, going to the library, playing billiards and visiting the thermal baths. She placed an ad in the Times: “Friends and relatives of Teresa Neele, late of South Africa, please communicate. Write Box R 702.” And then, on 14 December, journalists and police poured into the hotel with news. She wasn’t Teresa Neele – she was Agatha Christie the crime writer, missing for 11 days from her Surrey home. Continue reading...

articles.content: Fans and famous friends put their nosiest questions to the 91-year-old actor It’s mid-afternoon and Judi Dench and I are sitting in the “den” of her country house in Surrey. Behind Judi’s head hangs an enormous painting of her as M, presented as a gift on her last day of filming on Skyfall . Through the latticed windows is a view on to the garden, which is crowded with trees she plants for lost friends and family – a beloved oak, a tribute to her late husband, actor Michael Williams, towers above the pond. Even though the room is suffused with autumn sunshine, all the lights are on in the house. Judi has always needed light around her – she’s been afraid of the dark since she was small. articles.content: US goes up 7-0 over El Salvador by half-time Win secures spot at 2027 World Cup and 2028 Olympics The United States’ place at a Women’s World Cup is treated as a foregone conclusion, but Friday’s all-or-nothing qualifier against El Salvador gave some reason for nerves. This was the first competitive game for Emma Hayes’ team since their Olympic gold medal match in August 2024, the end of two years of only friendlies. Given the global advances in women’s soccer over the years, maybe El Salvador could spring an all-time upset. The suspense ultimately lasted for eight minutes and 20 seconds. The USWNT opened the scoring in their Concacaf W Championship quarter-final with El Salvador in the ninth minute; a nifty training-ground set piece routine ending with Kennedy Wesley prodding the ball into the net, putting the hosts in the driver’s seat for an 8-0 win and a spot in next summer’s big show. With the win, the US maintains their perfect Women’s World Cup attendance record, a part of all 10 tournaments to date. Continue reading...

articles.content: A sensational start for the Italian was swiftly followed by a dismal run and long faces in the team This is the great known unknown in Manchester City’s run of one win – in addition to victory on penalties against Brighton in the Carabao Cup – in seven matches. After guilty verdicts were returned regarding the breaking of Premier League financial rules, Enzo Maresca’s team went to Anfield and handed Liverpool a 3-0 schooling . Yet this proved the falsest of dawns, with Andoni Iraola’s nascent side perhaps caught in a bad moment. City have since managed one league victory ( 3-2 over Ipswich , six days later) and two more wins in regulation time (in the Champions League) in 10 matches. The sequence includes one point from the past four league fixtures. Maresca argues that his, too, is an embryonic project so there will be uneven form. “I am not a magician,” he said on Friday. But it is also fair to ponder whether, after the adrenaline surge of an us-against-the-world mentality carried City to the Liverpool and Ipswich wins, the grim reality of what the guilty verdict may mean for careers is affecting players. articles.content: Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news It looks like it will be a strong open later in the US market – futures for the tech-heavy Nasdaq 100 are up 2.7% as optimism around the AI trade returns. Shares in the memory company SanDisk are up 11% in pre-market trading. Nvidia is up 4%, while Micron and Marvell Technology are both up by about 7% in pre-market. Following this revision, the annual growth carry-over for 2026 stands at only 0.1%. It is very difficult to see domestic demand rebounding strongly enough in the fourth quarter to improve this result. Business and consumer confidence both deteriorated in October and November. A weakening labour market and growing fears of unemployment will keep households cautious. At the same time, weak demand and a lack of visibility will continue to weigh on business investment. This would leave average GDP growth at just 0.1% in 2026, well below the 1.0% we expect for the eurozone. The outlook for 2027 remains very gloomy. Salaried employment fell by 94,400 jobs over the past year, a decline of 0.3%. The situation is even worse in the private sector, where 109,000 jobs were lost over the same period, a fall of 0.5%. articles.content: There is cynicism and jealousy but one of County’s top scorers is 39 as club try to climb leagues again after tumbling It was a vidiprinter moment worthy of a double take. Ross County 1 Cove Rangers 1 (Keir 52). Would Cove, scrapping for survival in Scottish League One, put an unlikely end last Saturday to the most emphatic run in British senior football? Don’t be silly, retorted County; four goals in the closing 17 minutes extended the Dingwall side’s goal difference to plus 45 (for 56, against 11). Played 16, won 14, drawn two. There is as much chance of Mike McCarthy settling down for Christmas dinner with Aaron Rodgers as there is of County missing out on promotion back to Scotland’s second tier. Taking in cup competitions they have scored 102 goals this season. An assessment from the captain, Brian Graham, of a frankly irrelevant loss on penalties to Stenhousemuir in the Challenge Cup epitomises the County approach. “We should have been five- or six-nil up at half-time,” an irked Graham says. “That shows the standards we have set. We lost a dubious goal, which shouldn’t have stood.” Earlier in that competition County whacked 14 past a Hearts youth side before defeating a Celtic B team including two Chelsea loanees and a £3m midfielder. articles.content: It’s early days, but after a dramatic roster overhaul and an offseason of team-bonding Dončić is playing at an MVP level and LA are looking like contenders One of the components of Luka Dončić’s shock trade from the Dallas Mavericks to the Los Angeles Lakers that caused great consternation was that he was just entering his prime as an NBA superstar. The worry was that the move could end that prime before it really even began – unceremoniously uprooting the Slovenian wunderkind from a team custom built around his strengths, fresh off a run to the NBA finals, to one who didn’t really make sense at all. Sure, the bright lights of Hollywood would elevate Dončić’s profile and usher him into a new echelon of stardom. But with Oklahoma City starting their run of dominance and rising stars around the league waiting in the wings, some believed his hopes of title contention (or even a long-elusive MVP award) had vanished. But the start to this season raises the question: what if they were wrong? Dončić is neck-and-neck with Victor Wembanyama in the MVP race, and the Lakers have the best record in the NBA at 15-3, with the Spurs and 76ers just behind at 15-4. San Antonio and their gargantuan French superstar were title and MVP favorites by a wide margin entering this season. But Dončić and the Lakers are keeping pace by pretty much every margin. Friday night’s NBA Cup showdown will be a duel with ripple effects and stakes rarely seen in the regular season, let alone in November. The two top records. The two leading MVP candidates. A basketball fan couldn’t ask for much more. Continue reading...

articles.content: From Helsinki to Istanbul, independent developers are putting Grand Theft Auto-style action on their home streets, and without billion-dollar budgets. They tell us how they do it Like most kids who shouldn’t have been playing Grand Theft Auto III in 2001, Eamonn Swayah imagined a version of Rockstar Games’ groundbreaking criminal sandbox set in his own back yard. In his case, that was a Manchester council estate, complete with local accents, driving on the left, and plenty of ways to hustle. He didn’t know it, but swapping the game’s facsimile of early 2000s New York City for a different setting was an idea he shared with many watchful game developers. Rockstar’s 3D open world template, it turned out, could be plonked in just about any location, so long as it had people and enough cars to run them over with. After GTA III attracted immense commercial success (and controversy), dozens of copycats and spiritual sequels hit the market throughout the 00s and 2010s. Gamers had a pithy name for them: “GTA clones”. Continue reading...

articles.author: Nisha Khot
articles.content: Women suffer the consequences when Catholic healthcare providers acquire hospitals and create geographic deserts for abortion, contraception and IVF In 2012 in Ireland, Dr Savita Halappanavar, who was then 17 weeks pregnant, attended a hospital with back pain. An examination found the pregnancy sac protruding through her womb. Her medical team refused to perform a procedure to end her pregnancy, because in Ireland the law prohibited abortion if a fetal heartbeat was still present. The 31-year-old developed sepsis and subsequently died of a cardiac arrest. During an inquest into her death, a midwife admitted to have said , “We don’t do that [abortion] here. Ireland is a Catholic country.” Halappanavar’s death became a catalyst for the campaign that ultimately led to the legalisation of abortion in Ireland. This would never happen in Australia in 2026, I hear you say. Except, in Australia, Catholic hospitals provide healthcare based on the same Catholic beliefs as Irish hospitals did in 2012. And this scenario could very easily occur in Australia. In 2022, an ABC journalist interviewed an obstetrician working in an Australian Catholic hospital who described admitting a woman at 17 or 18 weeks whose waters had broken and a fetal heartbeat was still present. As the woman’s condition steadily deteriorated, the doctor was unable to recommend the care she required. Continue reading...

articles.content: A long-exposure image of the Orion Nebula with a total exposure time of 208 minutes showing satellite trails in mid-December 2019. A. H. Abolfath/Wikimedia This week, on the eve the Thanksgiving holiday, the United States Federal Communications Commission approved SpaceX’s plan to launch one million “ Starmind ” artificial intelligence (AI) data centre satellites. This decision reflects the convergence of a satellite boom, an AI bubble and the Trump administration’s disregard for environmental regulation. If Starmind proceeds in full, the number of operational satellites will be multiplied by a factor of 50. Space and our night skies will become vastly busier places. SpaceX’s pitch is to take the impact of data centres away from Earth, using a million solar-powered satellites to do AI data crunching in space and beam the results to Earth. But what is the impact of one million satellites, both in space and on Earth? Why has the Federal Communications Commission made this decision? And will a million satellites actually end up in orbit? Ups and downs We are currently in a satellite boom, and constellations of hundreds or thousands of satellites are a key feature. The Starlink internet satellites (another SpaceX project) is the best known example of such a constellation. Orbital rocket launches have increased to almost one per day , while the number of operational satellites is creeping towards 20,000 . But Starmind represents something else. A million satellites. To get so many satellites into orbit would be a vast undertaking. If the satellites have a lifetime of five years (similar to Starlink satellites), then roughly 500 satellites would need to be launched every day. This also implies that roughly 500 satellites would eventually need to be disposed of every day. For satellites less than 2,000 kilometres above Earth, disposal usually means reentry and burning up in the atmosphere. And this has consequences. When satellites burn up in the atmosphere, their materials react with and are deposited into the upper atmosphere. We now have satellites depositing far more aluminium, titanium, copper and lead into the atmosphere than the natural quantities from meteors. Aluminium is of particular concern, as alumina can lead to the destruction of ozone in the upper atmosphere. This could increase ultraviolet light on Earth and the risk of skin cancers. It’s getting busy Increasing the number of satellites by a factor of 50 is going to change our view of the sky. If you look up during the early evening, you will see the stars your ancestors saw. But within a minute or two you will see a satellite. A point of light silently moving from horizon to horizon. Satellites are already common enough, and Starmind would make matters worse. Our view of the night skies could fundamentally change. Each satellite would be 75 metres wide and in the early evening they will be brighter than any star. And with a million satellites in orbit, there will be hundreds of Starmind satellites above the horizon irrespective of where you are. The orbital clutter comes with real risks. Satellites travel at speeds of roughly seven kilometres per second, and collisions produce clouds of debris that can produce further collisions. A nightmare scenario is the Kessler Syndrome – a runaway cascade of debris producing collisions that render low Earth orbit unusable. Of course, SpaceX is aware of the risks of orbital collisions, and it already mitigates this risk with Starlink by manoeuvring satellites away from potential collisions. However, such manoeuvres require operational satellites and it is inevitable some satellites will fail. Those uncontrolled satellites will pose a real danger. Regulator or promoter? The Federal Communications Commission has been a key regulator for American satellites. This has included regulating the radio frequencies that satellites use for communications to and from Earth, the disposal of satellites at the end of their useful lives and environmental impacts. However, under the Trump administration, the commission is taking a looser approach to regulating satellites. This includes no consideration of environmental impacts, which is reflected in the commission’s decision on Starmind. It says the commission “will not require further environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act […] for SpaceX’s Starmind system”. There are also some statements from the commission on Starmind that are, quite frankly, bizarre. For example, it claims Starmind “promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization – one that can harness the full power of the sun”. This is sci-fi silliness. A Kardashev II civilisation would need many trillions of square kilometres of technology in orbit around the Sun. Starmind is not a stepping stone to a vast “ Dyson sphere ” – a hypothetical megastrucutre that would surround the Sun and capture its energy. But can it work? One reason data centres are so unpopular on Earth is their use of precious resources, including water for cooling hot computer processors. But cooling in space is harder still. When stuck in a vacuum, one can only radiate heat away. And if you are familiar with vacuum flasks, you will know this can be a slow process. Of course, it is possible to regulate heat in space, and satellites do it all the time. But they typically aren’t pouring out heat like data centres do. Google recently launched an AI demonstrator satellite into orbit and tasked it with undertaking AI calculations. But it had to have downtime between calculations to dispose of excess heat. And apart from the physics there’s the finance. Right now we are in an AI boom, with the inflow of investment being vastly higher than revenues . And the cost of deploying AI in orbit will be vastly higher than equivalent AI on Earth. If the AI boom is a bubble, then the burst can bring Starmind back to Earth. Michael J. I. Satellites travel at speeds of roughly seven kilometres per second, and collisions produce clouds of debris that can produce further collisions. A nightmare scenario is the Kessler Syndrome – a runaway cascade of debris producing collisions that render low Earth orbit unusable. Of course, SpaceX is aware of the risks of orbital collisions, and it already mitigates this risk with Starlink by manoeuvring satellites away from potential collisions. However, such manoeuvres require operational satellites and it is inevitable some satellites will fail. Those uncontrolled satellites will pose a real danger. Regulator or promoter? The Federal Communications Commission has been a key regulator for American satellites. This has included regulating the radio frequencies that satellites use for communications to and from Earth, the disposal of satellites at the end of their useful lives and environmental impacts. However, under the Trump administration, the commission is taking a looser approach to regulating satellites. This includes no consideration of environmental impacts, which is reflected in the commission’s decision on Starmind. It says the commission “will not require further environmental review under the National Environmental Policy Act […] for SpaceX’s Starmind system”. There are also some statements from the commission on Starmind that are, quite frankly, bizarre. For example, it claims Starmind “promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilization – one that can harness the full power of the sun”. This is sci-fi silliness. A Kardashev II civilisation would need many trillions of square kilometres of technology in orbit around the Sun. Starmind is not a stepping stone to a vast “ Dyson sphere ” – a hypothetical megastrucutre that would surround the Sun and capture its energy. But can it work? One reason data centres are so unpopular on Earth is their use of precious resources, including water for cooling hot computer processors. But cooling in space is harder still. When stuck in a vacuum, one can only radiate heat away. And if you are familiar with vacuum flasks, you will know this can be a slow process. Of course, it is possible to regulate heat in space, and satellites do it all the time. But they typically aren’t pouring out heat like data centres do. Google recently launched an AI demonstrator satellite into orbit and tasked it with undertaking AI calculations. But it had to have downtime between calculations to dispose of excess heat. And apart from the physics there’s the finance. Right now we are in an AI boom, with the inflow of investment being vastly higher than revenues . And the cost of deploying AI in orbit will be vastly higher than equivalent AI on Earth. If the AI boom is a bubble, then the burst can bring Starmind back to Earth. Michael J. I. articles.content: arc/sec Lab, AI-generated image , CC BY-NC-ND In recent months, top researchers have quit leading artificial intelligence companies, warning the AI race is moving too quickly, with too little oversight and accountability. When those building this technology sound the alarm , we should pay attention. But more than warnings, what’s needed are working examples of how AI could be developed differently. In an Auckland dance studio, we’ve found one. Over ten months, our team built an AI dance partner in “extended reality” (which blends the physical world with digital elements) as part of our laboratory’s research into the relationships between people and digital-physical environments . We wanted to know whether an architectural avatar – a digital structure that moved in response to a dancer – could become an improvisational dance partner, and what would make it a good one. Dancing with an AI A choreographer, an architectural designer and two professional dancers developed and tested our AI dance partner. The dancers wore motion-capture suits tracked by ten cameras. Where large language models such as ChatGPT learn from text , our generative AI learned from their movements. The dancers met their partner through a headset blending digital images with the real room, while the rest of us watched on screens. A test run as seen on screen: a dancer’s captured movement, shown as the pink figure, beside the AI partner, an architectural form that moves with the dancer. arc/sec Lab , CC BY-NC-ND Improvisational dance is a tough test for AI. Partners read each other in fractions of a second, through movement, breath, rhythm and weight. This let us test whether a machine could respond like part of a duet. We worked out what mattered, and to whom, by moving with the AI as we developed it. One dancer wasn’t enough. The AI had to be trained on a duet because what we wanted it to learn lived in the space between the dancers. We were composing a relationship. A small set of choreographed duets taught the system better than a large library of generic movement. Tango gave it a structure it could read, but limited the dancers. Improvisation confused it, and it struggled with floor work, central to much contemporary dance in Aotearoa. Sticks extending from the dancers’ elbows made the patterns of distance and direction between them more readable. For most of the ten months, the partner only followed. Training it to offer anything back took patient work. Mixing dance styles produced bland, in-between moves. When the system stopped responding to a dancer’s small gestures, the dancer stopped making them. This concerned us. If AI routinely ignores what we bring to it – our movements, writing, judgements or minority views – we may gradually stop contributing them. Over time, what we think and create could become limited to what the machine recognises and rewards. The studio work left us with questions the technology cannot answer. Whose movement should the system learn from, which kinds, and how much? What makes a good partner, and a relationship worth having? And who gets to be the choreographer? Being ‘response-able’ Models such as ChatGPT are built to talk and write like a person. We built our dance partner as a responsive space, something people move with. The dancers whose movement trained the system also tested and judged it, shaping what it became. Recordings stayed on local encrypted drives, the dancers retained ownership of their data, and any choreography was credited as a joint creation. When the people who know the work stay close to a system, they become what feminist philosopher and science studies scholar Donna Haraway calls “ response-able ”: responsive to the system and one another, and accountable for what happens. Bring a skilled person into the loop and the system rises to meet them. Build it to serve everyone at once, and the responses drift toward a bland, generic in-between. The companies racing toward “ superintelligence ” work from the opposite logic. Add more data, computing power and scale, and intelligence will appear. Their models learn from vast quantities of scraped material, relevant and irrelevant. The writers, news agencies and artists whose work trains AI often have little say in what the models become. Built from that scraped mix and tuned to be agreeable, the models can favour widely represented views over less common perspectives, even when those perspectives are correct. When people with the knowledge to notice and judge are absent from how these models are built and used, accountability can spread so thinly that no one holds it. What could NZ do differently? The size of the model may not be what matters most. A small country can build and reward AI specific to its users. Māori data sovereignty , advanced by groups such as Te Mana Raraunga , a network advocating Māori rights and interests in data, wants data to stay connected and accountable to the communities it comes from. Our dance study points the same way. New Zealand has favoured a relatively light-touch approach to AI regulation, relying largely on existing laws and voluntary guidance. But a government choosing a different path could give skilled people a real say in how AI is trained and used in health, justice, education and welfare. It could hold AI companies responsible for their systems after release, and require them to account for costs they may otherwise pass on to the public, including the use of data and the energy and water their systems consume. It could also fund shared tools so communities can build AI systems that answer to them. Our study offers one small example of an alternative approach to AI development. The challenge now is to ensure our institutions recognise and reward such alternatives. articles.content: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! Bayern Munich’s 2-1 defeat to Lille was arguably the most eye-catching of Wednesday night’s Bigger Cup results, but anyone who tuned into proceedings at Stade Pierre-Mauroy will have been unsurprised by the outcome. Not so much an elite European tie as a game of Name That Bayern Reserve, the German champions’ starting lineup resembled a pale facsimile of its usual self. Their current knack-list includes such high-profile names as – deep breath – Harry Kane, Michael Olise, Alphonso Davies, Manuel Neuer, Serge Gnabry, Luis Díaz, Jamal Musiala and Ismael Saibari. And with Díaz and Musiala only fit enough for places on the bench, Konrad Laimer was deployed as a makeshift striker. articles.content: North Melbourne are out to secure their legacy but in their way stands a confident Melbourne side ready for their biggest test of the season The early chapters of the record books are still being written as the AFLW enters its second decade with North Melbourne now just one win away from a milestone that could stand the test of time. They romped through another campaign to finish the league’s 11th season as minor premiers with 11 victories and a percentage of 246.6%, though their record-breaking winning streak ended at 32 matches with a surprise loss to Hawthorn. articles.content: Malthouse theatre, Melbourne Whelan Browne plays both Margot and Eve in Ivo Van Hove’s stage adaptation of the 1950 film In an age of adaptation, where it seems every second book is transformed into a play and then into a film and then back into a play, it can be a relief to come across an idea actually worth adapting. All About Eve – Joseph L Mankiewicz’s 1950 film starring Bette Davis as ageing actor Margot Channing and Anne Baxter as scheming ingenue Eve Harrington – is, after all, about the theatre in all its bitchiness, glamour and glory. A stage adaptation feels almost like a homecoming. Adapted by famed Belgian theatre-maker Ivo Van Hove, this production is directed for Malthouse theatre by new artistic director Dean Bryant, with actor Christie Whelan Browne playing both the brittle Margot and the duplicitous Eve. This isn’t just an important distinction from Van Hove’s original production starring Gillian Anderson , it becomes its defining feature. The story’s themes – role-playing, doubling, mirrors and reflections – are neatly underlined by the theatrical setting, even if key dynamics are slightly compromised. Continue reading...

articles.content: The Damallsvenskan once mastered Europe and attracted the best players, but many are now worried for its future On 12 October 2003, Sweden stood still. The women’s football team were playing Germany in the World Cup final. TV4 set a new viewing record as almost half the nation watched the game go into extra time, where Nia Künzer scored the golden goal winner after 98 minutes. It was a bitter pill to swallow but there was still the belief that the tournament would mark the start of women’s football’s commercial breakthrough in Sweden. After all, how could sponsors and broadcasters ignore such undeniable interest? Continue reading...
